analytic.title: Scheduling the Asynchronous Fixed-Priority tasks with Preemption Threshold

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Fixed-priority with preemption threshold (FPPT) is an important form of real-time scheduling algorithm. However, most of current research works concerning FPPT assume the task priorities are predefined and have a task model which constraints all tasks are released simultaneously. This presumption is too pessimistic. The major contribution of this paper is an appropriate schedulability analysis, based on response time analysis, for supporting FPPT scheduling on asynchronous task set in hard real-time systems. The simulation result illustrate that our approach can improve the breakdown utilization of asynchronous task set by 5%-27%.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Fixed-priority preemptive (FPP) scheduling algorithms [11] and fixed-priority non-preemptive (FPNP) scheduling algorithms [13] are two important classes of real-time scheduling algorithms. To obtain the benefits of both FPP and FPNP algorithms, there are several other algorithms trying to fill the gap between them. The fixed-priority with preemption threshold (FPPT) scheduling algorithm [19] is one of them. This paper extends the current work on FPPT in [19] by applying FPPT scheduling on the asynchronous task set.

Exact response time analysis of task sets in which the task phasings are given by offsets is in general much more complex than the analysis of arbitrarily phased tasks. This is a result of the difficulty to identify the critical instant for a task. It is pessimistic to assume that this situation will occur in systems in which the task phasings are fixed by offsets. Since the critical instant for a task in an offset related task set is difficult to identify, the worst case response time is found by analyzing the response times for each task instance within a hyper-period. The maximum response time of these instances is the worst case response time of that task.

The current methods to some extent handle offsets between tasks that belong to the same transactions. This paper describes new method that provide the exact response time of tasks with fixed offset under FPPT, then an algorithm to analyze the schedulability of FPPT on asynchronous task set (FPPT-AST) scheduling is provided, which exploit this new schedulability test. It does not however remove the inherent complexity of analysis of offset related task sets. Analysis of large task sets with many task instances within the hyper-period is still a problem.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. The next section presents the assumed computation model. The related work is introduced in Section 3. Section 4 presents our approach to carrying out the schedulability analysis for FPPT on asynchronous task set. In Section 5, experiments and results of FPPT-AST algorithm is given. Finally, the conclusion is made in Section 6.

div.head: Related Work
div.p: Wang and Saksenas schedulability analysis [19] is based on the response time analysis of each task. The worst-case response time analysis is an extension of the level-i busy period analysis [12], in which the response time is calculated by determining the length of busy period, starting from a critical instant.

The analysis of response times of asynchronous task instances can be performed through schedule simulation. This method has been discussed by e.g. Leung and Whitehead, [10], and Audsley [1]. The latter showed that the minimum interval for simulation of task sets is an interval as long as the hyper-period. Schedule simulation has to our best knowledge not been applied to task sets. That extension is however quite straightforward: A worst case has to be built, and a schedule simulation be performed, for each task instance within the hyper-period.

In [5], Palencia and Harbour developed Tindells method further. Their analysis handles task sets with arbitrary offsets and jitter and they also show how the method can be used to analyse tasks with pure precedence relations. Precedence relations are modelled using offsets and jitter that are dynamic in the sense that they vary during the course of the analysis. In Palencia and Harbours method the transactions are still assumed to be arbitrarily phased.

In [15], Ola Redell and Martin Torngren extended Palencias approach furthermore. Their analysis try to create the worst case conditions for the execution of each individual task instance within a hyper-period. The worst case is built by choosing release jitter of higher priority tasks appropriately. Given these conditions, the corresponding task instance response time is calculated using partly iterative algorithms. In Redells method all tasks have fixed phases to each other.

div.head: Terminology and assumptions
div.p: This study deals with the fixed priority preemptive scheduling of tasks in a real-time systems with hard constraints, i.e., systems in which the respect of time constraints is mandatory. The activities of the system are modeled by periodic tasks. The model of the system is defined by a task set Γ of cardinality n, Γ = {τ 1 , τ 2 , ..., τ n }. A periodic task τ i is characterized by a quadruplet (C i , T i , D i , O i ) where each request of τ i , called instance, has an execution time of C i , a relative deadline D i . T i time units separate two consecutive instances of τ i (hence T i is the period of the task). The k th instance of task τ i , denoted as J k i , arrive at
div.formula: A k i = O i + (k -1) • T i k is integer k ≥ 0 (1)
div.p: where A k i is the arrival time, O i denotes the offset. We will assume, without loss of generality, that the offsets are smaller than the task periods (O i ≤ T i ). If larger offsets are used, these can be normalized such that O normalized i = O i mod T i , and the analysis applied to the normalized task set. This is possible since different instances of the same task are indistinguishable from each other. The system is said schedulable if each instance finishes before its deadline.
We further assume that the total utilization of all tasks, U , is strictly less than 1. This will later be shown to be a necessary condition for the analysis.

The set of all possible priority orderings over Γ is given by ∆ Γ . Each γ∈∆ Γ consists of a set of n tuples (τ i , π i ), one per task, assuming π i = i, where π i denotes the priority level assigned to τ i and the smallest number is given to the task with highest priority.

For a task τ i in FPPT, before J k i begin execution, the interference caused by other tasks with regular priority higher than π i is possible; Once J k i starts actually, only the tasks with regular priorities higher than γ i can preempt J k i . Thus the staring time of J k i play a necessary role in the analysis of FPPT, so a notation S k i is introduce to denote it, S k i is used to represent the starting point of J k i , F k i denote the time point that J k i finish its execution. The analysis will be performed by studying the level-i busy period in which J k i executes. It is important to notice that we adopt the definition of a busy period given by e.g. Sun and Liu [17]. In their definition a level-i busy period starts and ends with a level-i idle point as opposed to the idle intervals that form the limits for a busy period in the definition by Lehoczky [12].

div.head: Schedulability Analysis for FPPT-AST
div.p: The analysis described here is in many parts similar to the analysis derived by Ola Redell and Martin Torngren in [15]. The difference lies in our assumption that all tasks have fixed preemption threshold to each other. The major contribution in the derivation described here lies in the analysis of the actually staring time of the analyzed task instance and the exact calculation of blocked time.

The method for deriving the worst case response time for a task is based on the calculation of worst case response times for all the individual task instances within a feasible interval [10]. Any feasible schedule of an asynchronous system is finally periodic from S n [3], S n is define iteratively as following:

div.head: J k i 's blocking time on other tasks
div.p: As we know, Wand and Saksena [19] assumed that the task contributing the maximum blocking time has just started before the first FPPT critical instant. When tasks has fixed different offset under FPPT, it might impossible to create the worst cases of the response time for respective tasks, because FPPT critical instant [7] may not exist. This assumption is too pessimistic to describe the exact schedule of asynchronous tasks under FPPT.

Let task τ l with the lower regular priority than π i , but with the higher preemption threshold than γ i . If the b th instance of τ l (denoted as J b l ) has influence on J k i , then J b l must start to execute before A b l . J b l start its execution, its priority could be upgraded to the higher preemption threshold, and J b l could block J k i in this scenario. This is to say, evaluation of S b l is the precondition of calculation the blocked time of J k i , S b l require another complicated analysis and calculation, then..., and so on, which might make the overall schedulability analysis iterative and even untractable in certain scenario.

Reversely, it is easy to decide whether the analyzed instance could block other task and evaluate the analyzed instance's blocking time for other tasks. In FPPT, each task has two priorities, regular priority π i and preemption threshold γ i . If π i = γ i , other tasks with the regular priority between π i and γ i are possible to be blocked by τ i , these tasks are represented as τ h , the number of instance could be blocked is denoted as η h . As for J k i , all the instance of τ h that arrive in the time interval [S k i , F k i ] might be blocked by J k i . And different instance experience different blocked time. Thus the blocked time B k,u i,h 1≤u≤η h of J u h can be formulated as:
div.formula: F k i -   (A u h -S k i ) - ∀j,πj <γi A u h -S k i T j • C j  (15)
div.p: For the task with the lowest priority τ min , no other tasks are able to block τ min , B min = 0; but τ min might block other tasks. If the analysis begin from the τ min by the sequence of priority order, thus no recursive calculation is possible.

div.p: In the course of derivation of equations mention above, there is no coherent constraints on the relations between task period T i and task deadline D i . Therefore, this new schedulability analysis approach can be applied to T i < D i , T i > D i , T i = D i and so on, all types of real-time task set. At the same time, the derivation procedure do not depend on any fixed-priority scheduling algorithms, thus this method can collaborate with all the fixed-priority scheduling policy, such as RM [11] and DM [14].

To compare the schedulability of a task set under different scheduling policies,we need a quantitative measurement. One possibility is to use the binary measure of schedulability,i.e., either a task set is schedulable or not. A better measure, and one that is commonly used is the notion of breakdown utilization [8]. The breakdown utilization of a task set is defined as the associated utilization of a task set at which a deadline is first missed when the computation time of each task in the task set is scaled by a factor. In this paper we use breakdown utilizations to measure schedulability.

We use randomly generated periodic task sets for our simulations. Each task is characterized by its computation time C i , its period T i , its deadline D i and its offset O i . We vary three parameters in our simulations: (1) number of tasks totaltasks, from 2 to 20; and (2) maximum period for tasks maxperiod, from 100 to 500; and (3) Offset/Period, from 0.1 to 0.9. For any given pair of totaltasks, maxperiod, and Offset/Period, we randomly generate 1000 task sets, and the simulating result is the average value over these 1000 task sets.

A task set is generated by randomly selecting a period, a deadline, an offset and computation time for each of the totaltasks. First, a period T i is assigned randomly in the range [1, maxperiod] with a uniform probability distribution function. Then,we assign a utilization U i in the range [0.1/totaltasks, 2.0/totaltasks], again with uniform probability distribution function. The computation time of the task is then assigned as T i * U i . Deadlines are assigned just as periods, and deadline of each task is unique. Finally, an offset O i is assigned randomly in the range [0, T i ] with a uniform probability distribution function.

For each randomly generated task set, we measure the breakdown utilization for each of (1) pure preemptive scheduling, (2) Audesley's algorithm [1], and (3) scheduling with preemption threshold. We do this by scaling the computation times to get different task set utilization, and then testing for schedulability. We then use binary search to find the maximum utilization at which the task set is schedulable under a particular scheduling algorithm. We note that our experiments are executed in the environment of Pentium 1.8G, 786M RAM, Redhat9 ( linux-2.4.20-8, gcc-3.4.2, X11, SPAK-0.3 ).

In figure 1 and figure 2 we show that the proportionally increased offsets have no corresponding improvement on schedulablitliy as the number of tasks varied. That results are shown for maxperiod = 100 and 200. In each case, we plot the different breakdown utilization values when using preemption threshold with varied offset/period values. As the number of tasks increases, the breakdown utilization tends to decrease. Another interesting phenomenon is that proportionally increased offset can not improve break- The reason for this is that with large number of tasks, and a small value of maxperiod, the computation times for all tasks are small.

In figure 3 and figure 4 we show that the variation of longest response time of each task as offset/period changed. That results are shown for totaltasks = 6 and 10. In each case, we plot the respective longest response time of each task when using preemption threshold with varied offset/period values. For lowest-and highest-priority tasks, offset augment has little influence on their longest response times. However for the medium-priority tasks, worst case response times fluctuate greatly as offsets increased. That result should not be surprising, because the tasks with the medium priority might undergo the more blocking from the lower-priority tasks and the more interference from the higher-priority tasks, variation of offset/period have the more notable effect on these tasks.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: We present a fixed-priority scheduling model with preemption threshold specialized for asynchronous task set. This model also bridges the gap between preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling and includes both of them as special cases. In this paper, using the concept of level-i busy period, we derive the equation for computing the worst-case response time of asynchronous periodic tasks in this model. Furthermore, based on the theoretical analysis we developed under the model, we proposed an efficient algorithm for finding optimal preemption threshold assignment for a task set with predefined priority. Finally, we present simulation results over randomly generated task sets showing our model achieves improvement of the schedulable utilization of task sets over preemptive cases.
